strengths: AIMCoT addresses a relevant problem with a coherent training-free framework combining context enhancement, entropy-based region selection, and dynamic visual insertion.
The reported improvements are consistent across three benchmarks, two 7B backbones, and both zero- and one-shot settings. Component ablations generally support the usefulness of CAG, AVP, and DAT.
The paper includes useful implementation-oriented material: pseudocode, hyperparameters, candidate-set ablations, threshold sensitivity, and latency measurements.
The comparison with ICoT is especially relevant, and the largest reported gains on LLaVA-W suggest that active region selection may be promising for open-ended tasks.
weaknesses: The claimed empirical support for approximate submodularity contains a sign error. With information gain defined as U(S)-U(S union {R}), diminishing returns requires U_s-U_s* >= U_l-U_l*, equivalently U_s*-U_s <= U_l*-U_l. Equation 17 tests the opposite inequality, so Table 6 does not support the stated conclusion or the theoretical motivation for greedy selection.

The AVP quantity is a reduction in next-token predictive entropy, not information gain in the usual mutual-information sense. Lower entropy need not imply more task-relevant evidence and can reward regions that make the model confidently wrong. No analysis connects this surrogate to answer correctness or grounding quality.

The principal results lack repeated trials, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite stochastic decoding and randomly sampled candidate regions. This is particularly concerning for LLaVA-W, which has only 60 examples and is evaluated using lexical ROUGE-L against reference responses; this weakly supports claims about open-ended reasoning quality.

Baseline and compute fairness are insufficiently established. CAG adds a separate image-description generation pass, while AVP performs multiple candidate lookaheads. There are no compute- or token-matched controls, and the statement that some baseline numbers are taken from prior work leaves unclear whether all systems use identical prompts, decoding, splits, and implementations.

The evidence motivating DAT is observational rather than causal: synchronization with attention shifts is measured post hoc and may correlate with other properties of successful responses. Attention mass is also sensitive to context composition and the growing number of visual tokens. Comparisons against stronger trigger policies are absent.

CAG may improve performance simply by providing an additional self-generated textual rationale, rather than by making attention maps more reliable. The paper does not directly evaluate attention localization quality or include an adequate description-only, compute-matched control isolating this mechanism.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the code/anonymized-link locations are blank in the supplied manuscript, and important details such as final-answer prompts, one-shot demonstrations, random seeds, exact evaluation splits, baseline configurations, and architecture-specific insertion mechanics are not fully specified.

Claims that the method produces more reliable, robust, or human-like reasoning exceed the evidence. Evaluation covers final-answer performance but not rationale faithfulness, visual grounding, or whether inserted regions causally support the answers. These issues require substantial correction and new controlled experiments before the work is sound enough for Findings.

strengths: The paper presents a clearly motivated, modular, training-free framework addressing region selection and insertion timing in interleaved multimodal reasoning. The topic is relevant to current vision-language research.

Evaluation covers two 7B backbones, three benchmarks, zero- and one-shot settings, component ablations, candidate-pool variants, hyperparameter sensitivity, and runtime. This is broader than a minimal empirical evaluation.
Reported gains are directionally consistent across all benchmark/backbone combinations, with particularly large improvements over ICoT on LLaVA-W using Chameleon-7B.

The paper is generally readable, and the appendices provide useful algorithmic, runtime, and diagnostic details. weaknesses: The central theoretical framing is not valid as stated. The proposed “information gain” is a difference between next-token entropies before and after inserting one observed crop; it is neither mutual information nor expected information gain, and lower next-token entropy need not mean a more accurate answer. A crop can make the model confidently wrong or merely sharpen an unrelated token. No experiment establishes that this surrogate reliably measures answer-relevant information.

The approximate-submodularity evidence does not justify the claimed optimization rationale. It tests only greedily constructed nested sets and one randomly sampled additional region, rather than the required condition over arbitrary nested sets and elements. Satisfaction rates near 61–72% do not establish a useful greedy approximation guarantee. The appendix also appears to reverse the entropy-reduction sign when expressing the tested marginal gain.

The main empirical evidence lacks uncertainty estimates or significance testing despite stochastic decoding with temperature 0.7 and sampling enabled. Several gains on Qwen2-VL are only 0.6–1.6 absolute points, so single-run results cannot support repeated claims of significant superiority.

LLaVA-W contains only 60 examples, and the paper replaces its usual model-judge evaluation with ROUGE-L against reference responses without validating that metric. Moreover, the DAT threshold is selected at the performance peak on this same benchmark, creating a serious risk of test-set tuning. Dataset-specific hyperparameter selection procedures and development splits are not reported.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed mechanisms. CAG adds an extra question-conditioned VLM pass that can itself infer answer-relevant content, but there is no matched-compute description/self-refinement control showing that gains arise from improved attention maps. DAT is not compared with random or frequency-matched insertion, so its benefit may reflect a different number of inserted regions rather than correctly detected “cognitive” moments.

The post-hoc DAT motivation is correlational and potentially circular: successful generations may produce different attention patterns, rather than synchronized insertions causing better answers. The reported Pearson correlation is weak (0.2166), while grouping by outcome quality does not resolve confounding.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The promised code/anonymized link is blank in the supplied manuscript; exact baseline prompts, answer extraction, seeds, dataset splits, and tuning protocol are missing. Table 5 is internally inconsistent for LLaVA-W: it reports NC=6, N=2, and M=1 even though the method defines NC=N+M. Baseline results are said to be copied from prior work “where applicable,” without identifying which entries were copied or demonstrating matched prompts and decoding budgets.

The ScienceQA description and citation appear inconsistent with the multimodal benchmark normally used in this literature: the manuscript attributes it to Saikh et al. and claims over 100,000 triples, whereas the widely used multimodal ScienceQA benchmark has roughly 21,000 questions and a different primary citation. This ambiguity makes the evaluated data and comparability unclear.

Claims such as “human-like,” “advanced capability,” and “advances the frontier” exceed the evidence. The study evaluates only two older 7B models, gives no qualitative error analysis beyond a favorable anecdote, and does not test whether the generated multimodal chains are faithful explanations rather than intervention artifacts. Substantial conceptual reframing, controlled experiments, repeated runs, and reproducibility repairs are needed before the work meets the Findings soundness threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent, training-free framework for interleaved multimodal reasoning. CAG, AVP, and DAT address identifiable limitations of attention-only region selection and fixed insertion triggers, and AVP’s entropy-based selection is an intuitive and practically useful heuristic.

The empirical coverage is broad: two substantially different 7B vision-language backbones, three benchmarks, zero- and one-shot settings, comparisons with several relevant CoT baselines, and component-level ablations. AIMCoT improves every reported backbone/benchmark/shot combination, with particularly substantial gains on the open-ended LLaVA-W benchmark.

The ablations generally support the architectural claims: removing each component degrades performance, the CAG/AVP factorial analysis helps separate their effects, and comparisons of attention-based, exploratory, selective-search, and segmentation-derived candidate pools provide useful design evidence.

The appendices contain valuable additional analysis, including hyperparameters, a sensitivity study for the trigger threshold, candidate-pool analyses, runtime measurements, and an explicit greedy-selection algorithm. Reported inference overhead relative to ICoT is moderate.

The work is clearly relevant to computational linguistics through multimodal language-model reasoning, grounding, and chain-of-thought construction. The manuscript is mostly well organized and its method is understandable.
weaknesses: The main results do not report repeated runs, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, despite stochastic decoding, random exploratory-region sampling, and several small absolute improvements—especially the 0.6–1.1 point gains on Qwen2-VL. Thus, repeated claims that improvements are “significant” are not established statistically.

The proposed “information gain” is not expected information gain or mutual information: it is the reduction in next-token predictive entropy after adding a crop. Lower entropy can reflect increased confidence without increased correctness, including confidently reinforcing an erroneous hypothesis. The paper does not measure calibration or directly validate that entropy-selected regions contain more answer-relevant evidence than alternatives.

The appendix’s claimed evidence for approximate submodularity appears to use the wrong inequality direction. Given its definitions, diminishing returns in entropy reduction requires U_s−U_s* >= U_l−U_l*, whereas Eq. 17 tests U_s*−U_s >= U_l*−U_l. These are opposite conditions. Consequently, the binomial tests do not support the stated submodularity interpretation or any associated motivation for the greedy procedure.

The evidence motivating DAT is correlational and potentially confounded. On only 60 LLaVA-W examples, synchronization with attention shifts may covary with response length, insertion count, or answer structure. The DAT ablation compares against a newline trigger but lacks stronger controls such as random or periodic triggers matched for insertion frequency. Moreover, the default threshold is selected at the peak of a sweep on LLaVA-W, with no clearly separate development set, raising test-set tuning concerns.

Evaluation on the small, open-ended LLaVA-W benchmark relies only on ROUGE-L against GPT-4V-generated references. This metric can poorly reflect semantic answer quality, so the largest reported gains need confirmation through human evaluation or a validated semantic/judge-based metric.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently documented. The paper states that previously reported numbers are used “where applicable” but does not identify which entries were rerun, whether decoding configurations and prompt budgets were matched, or whether all methods received comparable extra generation and visual-token compute. CAG also generates a question-conditioned description, so part of its benefit may come from additional reasoning or answer leakage rather than improved attention maps specifically.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the manuscript: the displayed code links are blank, and important details such as random seeds, number of runs for the main tables, exact prompts and demonstrations, split/sample counts, baseline-specific settings, and software versions are missing. The claimed supplementary code may mitigate this, but the paper itself does not establish robust replication conditions.

Some conclusions are overstated. The experiments support benchmark improvements, but not the stronger characterization of AIMCoT as more “human-like,” nor do generated rationales necessarily constitute faithful or interpretable reasoning. The complexity discussion also idealizes crop encoding and cache reuse and omits peak-memory and throughput measurements.

strengths: AIM-CoT addresses a relevant problem in multimodal reasoning through a coherent trigger-select-insert framework combining query-conditioned descriptions, active region selection, and dynamic insertion timing.

The empirical scope is substantial: three VQA benchmarks, four diverse VLM backbones, zero- and one-shot settings, significance tests, component ablations, robustness studies, and latency measurements.

Reported improvements are consistent across all evaluated settings, and the ablations generally support the practical utility of each component. The gains over ICoT are particularly meaningful on LLaVA-W and weaker fixed-resolution backbones.

The paper investigates selected-region quality in addition to final task performance and provides useful qualitative examples, candidate-source analyses, adaptive triggering experiments, and adversarial-noise tests.
The method is training-free and appears practically implementable, with reported latency below 1.36 times that of ICoT under the tested configurations.
weaknesses: The central “information gain” characterization is technically misleading. The score is merely the change in entropy of a single next-token predictive distribution after adding a region; it is not mutual information and can reward irrelevant or misleading evidence that makes the model confidently wrong. No accuracy- or calibration-based analysis tests this failure mode.

The claimed theoretical justification contains an apparent sign error. With uncertainty U defined as entropy and gain as U_before minus U_after, diminishing returns requires U*_s−U_s <= U*_l−U_l, whereas Equation 14 tests the opposite inequality. Consequently, Table 16 does not establish approximate submodularity or justify the stated greedy approximation/global-optimality claims.

The evidence for DAT's interpretation as detecting a “cognitive need” for vision is correlational and weak: it is based on one backbone and the 60-example LLaVA-W benchmark, with Pearson r=0.2166 and p=0.048. Attention-mass changes are also confounded by changing context length and inserted visual tokens. The DAT ablation supports practical utility, but not the stronger mechanistic claim.

CAG's causal explanation is insufficiently controlled. Generating and appending a query-conditioned image description adds substantial test-time computation and may directly expose answer-relevant text; comparisons against length-matched captions, additional deliberation, or equal-compute baselines are absent. Thus the gains cannot confidently be attributed to correcting text-vision granularity or refining attention.

The semantic-region evaluation is underspecified and potentially invalid as described: vanilla SAM does not ground textual mentions by itself, yet the paper says it generates masks for entities mentioned in questions and ground-truth answers without explaining the grounding prompts, annotations, or intermediate model. Using answer-derived entities also makes this only a limited proxy for independently judged relevance.

Evaluation and statistical reporting do not adequately address stochasticity. Decoding uses sampling with temperature 0.7, but seeds, repeated runs, variance, and stability across generations are not reported. One-sided instance-level tests on a single sampled run do not establish robustness to decoding randomness, and no correction is discussed for the many comparisons.

Hyperparameters are tuned separately by dataset, including the DAT threshold, but the tuning data and protocol are not specified. The one-shot exemplar selection, exact benchmark splits and main sample counts, baseline reimplementation details, model checkpoints, and hardware are also missing or unclear.

LLaVA-W contains only 60 examples and is assessed with ROUGE-L against GPT-4-generated references, which is a weak measure of open-ended answer quality. The GPT-4V region-preference and hallucination evaluations lack model-version details, repeated judging, human validation, and agreement analysis.
The manuscript claims that code is available but provides no URL or artifact. Together with the missing procedural details, this currently prevents adequate reproduction.

The paper contains questionable dataset documentation: its ScienceQA description and citation appear inconsistent with the commonly used multimodal ScienceQA benchmark. It also lacks a limitations section and overstates several empirical observations as theoretical or cognitive conclusions.

Overall, the empirical results are promising enough to approach Findings, but the incorrect theoretical argument, ambiguous evaluation procedures, and missing controls leave the soundness and reproducibility case unresolved. A revision could become suitable for Findings by correcting or removing the theory, adding equal-compute and calibration controls, and fully specifying and releasing the evaluation pipeline.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in multimodal reasoning: selecting useful visual regions and deciding when to insert them into an interleaved chain of thought. The proposed trigger-select-insert framework is clearly organized and reasonably motivated.

The empirical study is broad, covering three benchmarks, four VLM backbones, zero- and one-shot settings, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, significance tests, runtime measurements, and several diagnostic experiments.
The reported results are consistently better than the included baselines. Ablations indicate that CAG, AVP, and DAT each contribute, while the gains over ICoT are especially substantial on LLaVA-W.
The paper is generally readable, and the appendices provide useful implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, robustness tests, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central theoretical characterization is not valid as stated. The entropy difference for a particular observed crop is not mutual information or information gain in the usual information-theoretic sense; it lacks an expectation over possible observations and can be negative. Moreover, the neural-model set function is not shown to be monotone or submodular. Finding the diminishing-returns inequality on only 62–81% of tested instances does not establish an approximation guarantee for greedy selection. The paper should present AVP as a heuristic unless it supplies a correct formal result.

The evidence for DAT does not establish that attention shifts identify a causal need for visual evidence. The reported correlation is weak (r=0.2166, p=0.048), and the group analysis defines synchronization using response-relative top-quantile shifts and then relates it to response quality. This is at best associational. Controlled interventions at matched generation positions or comparisons against learned, random, entropy-based, and frequency-matched triggers are needed.

Hyperparameters appear to be tuned directly against benchmark performance, including dataset-specific DAT thresholds, but no validation split or tuning protocol is identified. This creates a material risk of test-set adaptation, particularly for the small LLaVA-W benchmark. The adaptive threshold is evaluated only after comparison with the tuned fixed threshold and is not clearly the method used for the headline results.

The experimental comparison is insufficiently controlled. CAG adds an answer-relevant, query-conditioned description and additional model computation, but there is no equal-compute comparison with ordinary caption augmentation, self-refinement, or an additional inference pass. Consequently, improvements attributed to attention refinement may instead arise from supplying a generated textual rationale. The paper also says some baseline numbers are taken from prior work without identifying which ones or establishing fully matched prompts and decoding settings.

Several auxiliary evaluations are under-specified or weak proxies. Vanilla SAM does not ground textual entities, yet the construction of SAM masks for entities in the question and answer is not explained. The GPT-4V preference study has no human validation, model/version details, repeated judging, or agreement analysis. These results therefore do not substantiate the paper's stronger claims about human-centered relevance.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate. The manuscript claims that code is available, but the code URL is blank. Random seeds, sampled-instance identities, the region-grounding procedure, baseline reproduction details, GPT-4V configuration, and repeated-run variability are missing. This is especially concerning because decoding uses sampling at temperature 0.7 while results appear to come from single runs; item-level significance tests do not account for generation randomness.

The evaluation uses ROUGE-L against reference responses for LLaVA-W, which is not a convincing measure of open-ended answer quality and can reward lexical overlap rather than correctness. A standard judge-based evaluation, preferably supplemented with human assessment, is needed. More generally, testing is limited to VQA-style datasets, so claims about vision-language reasoning and dynamic cognitive need are broader than the evidence supports.

Overall, the reported empirical pattern is promising, but invalid theoretical claims, possible benchmark-level hyperparameter tuning, missing controls, and incomplete reproducibility prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current form. These issues require important but feasible revisions rather than fundamental reconstruction.

strengths: AIM-CoT addresses a clear, relevant problem in multimodal reasoning: deciding both which visual regions to insert and when to insert them during generation. The trigger-select-insert framework is coherent and technically interesting.

The empirical evaluation is broad: three benchmarks, four substantially different VLM backbones, zero- and one-shot settings, component ablations, significance tests, threshold sensitivity, robustness stress tests, and latency measurements. The consistent improvements over ICoT provide credible evidence that the overall system is useful.

Ablations across multiple backbones generally support contributions from CAG, AVP, and DAT rather than attributing all gains to one component. The adaptive-trigger and efficiency results also improve the practical relevance of the work.

The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and generally explains the framework and its motivation well. The contribution is directly relevant to computational linguistics research on multimodal reasoning and grounded generation.
weaknesses: The theoretical characterization of AVP is not sound as written. A difference in next-token predictive entropy is not generally information gain or mutual information and can reward increased confidence in an incorrect prediction. Moreover, Appendix I.4 appears to reverse the sign of the entropy difference in Equation 14 relative to the marginal gain defined earlier. The reported 61–72% empirical satisfaction rates neither establish submodularity nor yield a greedy approximation guarantee, especially because gains can be negative and monotonicity is not shown. Claims of greedy optimality or theoretical support should therefore be removed or substantially revised.

The evidence for DAT does not isolate timing quality from insertion frequency. Its motivating analysis is correlational and potentially confounded by response content, length, and the baseline's newline-triggered insertions. The ablation compares DAT only with the static newline trigger; count-matched random triggers, periodic triggers, and oracle or retrospective controls are needed to demonstrate that attention shifts identify uniquely useful moments.

CAG generates a query-conditioned description that can itself contain answer-relevant inferences, as the example illustrates. The experiments do not adequately separate improved attention alignment from extra inference-time computation, self-refinement, or direct answer leakage through the generated description. Controls using length-matched text, an ordinary caption, or the description without AVP candidate construction would sharpen the causal claim. The small arithmetic differences labeled 'super-additivity' also lack uncertainty estimates or significance testing.

The auxiliary evidence-selection evaluations are insufficiently specified. SAM does not directly produce masks for textual entities, yet the procedure used to ground entities from the question and ground-truth answer is not described. The GPT-4v evaluation lacks an exact model version, decoding settings, repeated judgments, and human validation; using the ground-truth answer to construct reference masks also weakens the claim that these evaluations measure human-like selection independently.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract says code is available but supplies no URL, while important details such as random seeds, software/model revisions, hardware, sampling protocol, exact baseline reproduction procedure, and some attention aggregation choices are missing or scattered. The ScienceQA citation and description also appear to refer to a different scholarly-QA resource rather than the standard multimodal ScienceQA benchmark, making the evaluated dataset ambiguous.

Because generation uses sampling with temperature 0.7, single-run paired significance tests capture variation across examples but not variability across decoding runs. It is also unclear which baseline numbers were newly reproduced versus imported from prior work, limiting confidence in the fairness of the comparisons. Overall, the empirical system appears promising enough for Findings, but the theoretical and causal claims should be narrowed and the reproducibility gaps corrected before a main-conference recommendation.
